title: AI data startup Micro1 reaches $500M gross run rate amid AI training boom
content:
The near-bottomless demand for unique AI training data from top labs and corporations is driving a massive boom for a cohort of data-labeling startups.
One of these fast-growing businesses is Micro1, a four-year-old startup that expanded its gross annual run rate from $100 million to $500 million over the past eight months, according to a person familiar with the company. Like its peers that hire domain experts such as doctors, lawyers, and scientists on a contract basis, Micro1 retains roughly 60% to 70% of that figure, putting its net annual run rate between $150 million and $200 million.
While Micro1 still lags competitors like Mercor (which hit $2 billion in gross annualized revenue this summer) and Handshake (which reached $1 billion earlier this year), the startup’s revenue growth shows that there is more than enough demand to support multiple players supplying AI training data.
The rapid growth is bound to continue, with some researchers hypothesizing that future AI spending on data could rival spending on compute.
That outlook bodes well for Micro1, which is seeing its contract sizes grow at an accelerated pace and expects its margins to expand over time. The startup is increasingly generating synthetic data without human involvement, such as by creating automated descriptions of video content. Additionally, some of the data it generates can be sold to multiple customers, driving gross margins for this “off-the-shelf” data as high as 80% to 90%, a person familiar with the startup’s finances told TechCrunch.
Selling the same datasets to multiple clients has sparked recent controversy, with critics arguing that distributing off-the-shelf data to Chinese AI developers helps make their models as powerful as top U.S. models.
Micro1’s founder, Ali Ansari, said last month on X that unlike some of its competitors, the startup doesn’t sell its data to Chinese model makers. “Some human data companies work with foreign adversaries. [A]nd the results show today in Kimi K3. We believe it’s shameful to claim American AI dominance desires while selling millions worth of data to countries that we are in adversarial competition with.”
Like Mercor, Micro1 began as an AI recruiting startup. But after noticing that data-labeling clients were using his AI platform to vet and recruit engineers for annotation, Ansari decided to pivot and enter the data-labeling business, too.
Ansari previously told TechCrunch that in addition to having its experts evaluate model outputs — a concept known as reinforcement learning gyms — the company is building a robotics pre-training dataset by having hundreds of generalists record everyday object interactions in their homes.
Micro1 raised its Series A at a $500 million valuation last September, and TechCrunch understands that the startup may have recently raised another round at a significantly higher valuation.
Micro1 didn’t respond to a request for comment.

report.summary: Micro1 hits $500M gross run rate, showing booming demand for AI training data and data-labeling startups.
report.background: AI labs and large corporations need massive amounts of unique, high-quality data to train frontier models, fine-tune them, and evaluate outputs. This has created a gold rush for data-labeling startups that recruit doctors, lawyers, scientists, and other domain experts on contract. Micro1 started as an AI recruiting platform before pivoting into data labeling, and it has grown from $100 million to $500 million in gross annual run rate in just eight months. While it still trails competitors like Mercor and Handshake, the rapid growth signals that demand for training data is vast and expanding. Researchers even speculate that future AI spending on data could rival spending on compute, fueling continued investment in annotation, synthetic data, and evaluation services.
key_points: Micro1's gross annual run rate jumped from $100 million to $500 million in eight months, with net run rate between $150 million and $200 million after retaining 60–70%. This puts it among fast-growing data startups, though still behind Mercor and Handshake, proving rapid scaling is possible in training-data services.

The boom is driven by AI labs and enterprises needing unique, high-quality data for model training. Researchers speculate future AI spending on data could rival compute budgets. Multiple billion-dollar players exist simultaneously, indicating demand is not winner-take-all and contracts are growing faster than before.

Micro1 is expanding synthetic data and reusable 'off-the-shelf' datasets, including automated video descriptions. Because such data can be sold to several customers, gross margins reach 80–90%, higher than custom annotation work. This strategy could improve profitability while raising concerns about data reuse and model homogenization.

Selling reusable data to multiple buyers has drawn criticism, especially when it reaches Chinese developers. Founder Ali Ansari publicly said Micro1 does not sell to Chinese model makers, unlike some rivals, claiming such sales contradict American AI dominance. This highlights geopolitical tensions in AI data supply chains.

Beyond annotation, Micro1 is building robotics pre-training data from home recordings and running 'reinforcement learning gyms' where experts evaluate outputs. The company raised a Series A at $500 million valuation and may have completed another round at a higher valuation, signaling investor confidence.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Micro1's growth reinforces that high-quality data is a critical, monetizable layer alongside compute. Large labs will increasingly rely on specialized suppliers for human expertise, synthetic data, and evaluation services, creating new business models and pricing dynamics. Developers benefit from better underlying data and evaluation tools, but may face rising costs or vendor lock-in. Regular users will see capable models, yet the off-the-shelf data trade raises privacy, bias, and national-security questions. Whether to restrict data exports may become a key policy issue as nations compete in AI.
report.tools: For hands-on exploration, try Label Studio for custom annotation workflows, Argilla for data quality and feedback, and distilabel for building synthetic data pipelines. Watch Hugging Face Datasets for reusable training data, and the TRL library for reinforcement learning with human feedback. These open-source tools mirror parts of Micro1's stack, though not its proprietary expert network.
